topic: Massage for netball and basketball players

slides.headline: Calves wrecked after court training?
slides.sub: How remedial massage fits into a netball or basketball season.

slides.title: Courts are hard on legs
slides.body: Jumping, landing, sprinting and sudden stops load your calves, feet, quads and hips heavily. Preseason ramps that up fast, so tightness and heavy legs are common in the first few weeks.

slides.title: What massage can help with
slides.body: Remedial massage can ease that tight, heavy feeling and help you move more comfortably. Effects are usually short term, which is fine when your goal is getting through a demanding training week.

slides.title: Time it around games
slides.body: Deep work right before a game can leave muscles feeling flat. Most players prefer lighter work a day or two out, and firmer sessions after games or on lighter training days.

slides.title: It complements, not replaces
slides.body: Massage works well alongside landing practice, calf and hip strength, and sensible training load. It won't replace them. Think of it as one part of keeping your legs ready for the season.

slides.title: When to see a physio instead
slides.body: A rolled ankle, a knee that gives way, sudden sharp pain, swelling or pain that won't settle needs an assessment first. Our team refers between massage and physio when needed.

slides.headline: Keep your legs court-ready
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy tailor each session to your training week and where you're feeling it. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Preseason court training back on and your calves already feel like concrete?

Netball and basketball ask a lot of your legs: jumping, landing, sprinting and stopping on a dime. Tight calves, heavy quads and sore feet are common as training ramps up.

Remedial massage can ease that tight, heavy feeling and help you move more comfortably. Timing matters: lighter work a day or two before games, firmer sessions afterwards. It sits well alongside landing practice, strength work and sensible training load, not instead of them. A rolled ankle, swelling or a knee that gives way needs a physio assessment first.
